*86. SHRI    NARENDRA    MOHAN:    Will    the    Minister   of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state:

27

(c) if so, what measures Government propose to adopt in this regard

from countries like China, Singapore, et c. whose qualitatively better goods 
are available in the market at much cheaper price? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MAR AN): (a) to (c) India has been following a continuous 
policy of removal of restrictions on imports since 1991. Tariff line-wise 
import policy was first announced on 31.3.1996. As on that date, import of 
6161 tariff lines (at 10 digit level) out of the total number of 10202 tariff lines 
(at 10 digit level) was free. Import restrictions on 488 tariff lines (at 10 digit 
level) were removed during the period 1.4.96 to 31.3.97. Another 391 tariff 
lines (at 8 digit level) were freed during the period 1.4.97 to 13.4.98 and 894 
tariff lines (at 8 digit level) were freed on 1.4.99. Quantitative restrictions on 
714 items were removed on 31.03.2000 and import restrictions on the 
balance 715 items are required to be removed by 31.03.2001. 
Thus it is evident that QRs are not being removed for the first time. In the 
liberalized import regime the domes tic industry will be obliged to face 
competition from imports subject to the applicable rate of customs duty. 
However, removal of QRs has not led to  any surge in imports. The rate of 
growth of imports which stood at 36.40% in 1995-96 has come down 
progressively over the years to 13.2% in 1996-97, 11% in 1997-98, 14.2% in 
1998-99, 13.6% in 1999-2000 and 10.6% during April—December 2000. In 
view of the inelastic demand for petroleum products, if non-oil imports alone 
are taken into consideration, import growth rates are even lower. The 
provisional non-oil import growth rate during April—December, 2000 has 
been (-)8.3%. 
The imports are being closely monitored and the Government is 
determined to ensure that imports do not cause any serious injury to the 
domestic producers. Some of the recent  measures towards that end are as

Free Trade Agreement are as follows:—  
1. The Agreement envisages phasing out of tariff on all products except 
for a limited number of items in the Negative List, over a period of time. 
2. The Rules of Origin specify that domestic value addition requirement 
should be 35%. If the raw materiaM nputs are sourced from each other's 
country, the value addition in the expor ting country has to be at least 25% 
within the overall limit of 35%. The criterion of "substantial transformation" 
has been provided in the Rules. The goods must undergo transformation at 4 
digit level of the Harmonized System. 
3. The Agreement provides for sufficient safeguards to protect the 
domestic industry. In particular, if the import of any product causes or 
threatens to cause serious injury to the domestic industry, the contracting 
parties can suspend provisionally without discrimination 
32 

[27 February, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
the  preferential  treatment   accorded  to  the  product  under  the 
Agreement. 
4. Further, the Agreement provides that the contracting parties shall be 
free to apply domestic legislation to restrict imports, in cases where prices are 
influenced by unfair trade practices like subsidies or dumping. Also, in the 
case of balance of payments difficulties, Contracting Parties may suspend 
provisionally the preferential treatment as to the quantity and value of 
merchandize permitted to be imported under the Agreement. 
The FTA has been made operative by the issuance of Customs Notification 
on 1st March, 2000. 
The FTA will accelerate the development of national economies, promote 
mutually beneficial bilateral trade and strengthen intra-regional economic 
cooperation.

policy measures for poverty alleviation, rural development, rural employment

(a) whether keeping best interest in vciw, a think tank has suggested that

suggestions have been made for creation of a 'livelihood box' under the 
Agreement on Agriculture during the ongoing mandated negotiation on 
agriculture in WTO. 
(b) and (c) India in its negotiating proposals submitted to the WTO for the 
ongoing negotiations under the Agreement on Agriculture, has  emphasised  
that  for  large  agrarian  developing  countries  like 
102

India, food security is an important and integral element of national security 
and has demanded the creation of a "Food Security Box" so as to take care 
of its food security and livelihood concerns and has interalia sought

country members for allevation of poverty, rural development, rural 
employment and diversification of agri culture. However, the items such as

White Paper on WTO 
582. SHRI V.P. DURAISAMY : Will the Minister of 
COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to bring out a White Paper on WTO and 
agriculture, detailing the expectations, the experience and the stand it plan to 
take in renegotiating the agreement; and 
103 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2001] 
(b) what steps Government would take  to deal with threats that are 
inherent in the WTO Agreement? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI 
MURASOLI MARAN): (a) The Government have already announced its 
National Agricultural Policy and have also put on the website of the 
Department of Commerce a broad position paper on the WTO Agreement on 
Agriculture and the Indian proposals as submitted by India in the WTO for 
the ongoing mandated negotiations under the Agreement on Agriculture. 
(b) The WTO agreements have prov ided a predictable rule based 
multilateral trading system which protects developing countries from the 
bilateral pressures of the developed coun try partners. By virtue of signing of 
WTO agreement, India is automatically entitled to get the" most favoured 
nation (MFN) and national treatment from all WTO members for its exports. 
Being a fully democratic organisation, with equal voting rights to each 
member, India is assured of a say in the multilateral rule making process. 
Under the ongoing mandated negotiations on the Agreement on Agriculture, 
India in its proposals submitted to WTO, has sought flexibility in the 
implementation of its domestic policies so as to take care of its food security, 
livelihood, rural development and poverty alleviation concerns. India in its 
proposals, has also demanded substantial reduction in domestic support, 
elimination of export subsidies, substantial reductions in tariffs including 
elimination of tariff peaks and tariff escal ation so as to get meaningful market 
access for its agricultural products in th e developed country markets. In the 
wake of removal of QRs as were maintained on Balance of Payment grounds, 
Government have also put in place a suitable mechanism for monitoring the 
import of sensitive items and are committed to provide adequate protection to 
the domestic producers by resorting to various WTO compatible measures 
which include appropriate calibration of applied tariffs within the bound 
tariffs, anti-dumping and safeguard action and imposition of countervailing 
duties under certain specified circumstances.

(c) and (d) The Income-tax Act prescr ibes a statutory procedure for 
recovery of taxes. The recovery of the outstanding tax is a continuous 
process. The process starts after the demand falls due after 30 days of the 
service of the demand notice. Thereafter, action is taken by Assessing Officer

attaching bank accounts etc. In difficult cases, matter is referred to tax 
Recovery Officer who takes various coercive measures as per the Act. The 
recovery action taken by the Assessing Officer and TRO is closely monitored 
by the higher Income Tax Authorities. No time limit can be fixed for 
recovery of dues for the cases which arc under dispute, as the asscssccs 
generally do not pay up the contested demands of taxes considered due by

Officers to liaise with Control Room. They have also been advised to 
immediately ensure resumption of Banking Services in the affected area. A 
Special State Level Bankers* Committee (SLBC) meeting was held at 
Ahmedabad on 09.02.2001. After deliberations, the following guidelines were 
issued by RBI on 12.02.2001 (Statement enclosed) regarding relief to 
earthquake-affected people. (See below) 
(A) Loan Classification status in case of borrowers affected by the 
earthquake would be frozen on an 'as-is-where-is' basis up till 31.03.2003. 
(i) In regard to standard assets, no demand for recovery to be made for 
two years. 
(ii) In regard to loans not classified as standard assets, no penalties to be 
levied in the even of non-receipt of repayments of due during the 
next two years.

per annum till 31.03.2003 and thereafter normal rate of 
interest would be charged.

employmc-rS. and small road transporter etc. would be sanction special limits 
upto Rs. 1 lakhs for restoration/rehabilitation of their businesses at interest 
rates not exceeding PLR. 
(C) Banks would grant loans, upto Rs. 2 lakhs at interest rate not 
exceeding PLR for repairs/reconstructio n of houses/shop damaged by the 
earthquake. 
(D) In regard to advances to SSI, business, trade and industry, banks 
would consider sanction of additional limits. The interest on rescheduled loans 
will be charged @ 10% per annum at simple rate upto 31.03.2003 and 
thereafter, at PLR. The interest on additional

(G) No processing fees will be charged by the banks from the 
affected beneficiaries.

small traders, small business, self employed and small road

Scarcity of Irrigation Water 
681. SHRI K. M. SAIFULLAH: 
SHRIMATI VANGA GEETHA: 
Will the Minister of WATER RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether India will be among the countries worst hit by water scarcity 
which will be primary global concern in the new millennium; and 
(b) if so, the steps proposed to ensure  that the country would not face 
seep cutbacks in the supply of irrigation water? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF WATER 
RESOURCES (SHRIMATI BIJOYA CHAKRAVARTY): (a) India received 
average annual precipitation of about 4000 Billion Cubic Meter (BCM). Out 
of this about 1869 BCM appears as runoff in the various rivers of the 
country. On an average water availability in the country remains more or less 
fixed according to the natural hydrological cycle. According to international 
criteria any situation of yearly water availability of less than 1000 cu.m. per 
capita is considered as scarcity cond ition. It is estimated that due to 
increasing population, the average annu al per capita water availability may 
come down from about 1869 cu.m. at present to 1350 cu.m. by 2025 A.D. at 
the national level. Due to spatial variability of rain in the country and also 
because of variation in population de nsity, per capita average annual 
availability of water in different basins also varies from 14,057 cu.m. in 
Brahmaputra to 307 cu.m. in Sabarmati basin. Further, the temporal 
variability in the rainfall creates scarc ity of water in certain years. The 
requirement of irrigation water in different parts of the country upto 2025 
A.D. can be met through optimal sustainable development and efficient 
utilization of the renewable water resources through a combination of 
measures like construction  of appropriate  storages, ground water 
development, 
197 

RAJYA SABHA [27 February, 2001] 
watershed management, artificial recharge of ground water etc., as 
appropriate for particular regions. 
(b) Construction of dams and storages on the rivers improves the 
utilization of river flows. A live storage capacity of 177 BCM has been 
created by construction of large dams upto 1995. Projects to add an additional 
storage capacity of about 75 BCM are under construction and 132 BCM are 
under planning. The replenishable ground water is of the order of 432 BCM, 
out of which about 154 BCM has been developed foi use. With the help of 
these storages and other minor irrigation schemes an irrigation potential of 90 
Mha has been created upto the end of the Eighth Plan against the ultimate 
irrigation potential of 139.9 Mha in the country. For the early completion of 
on- going projects Government of India is extending assistance to the States 
under Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme. 
Government of India is also promoting rainwater harvesting through 
Watershed Management Programme, artific ial recharge of ground water and 
roof-top rainwater harvesting under the sector reform project of Accelerated 
Rural Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development, 
for which technical and financial a ssistance is provid ed to the State 
Governments and other implementing agencies. Central Ground Water Board 
has also taken up pilot studies for artificial ground water recharge. A National 
Water Policy already exists which provides for planning and management of 
country's water resources on a sustainable basis. 
As a long term measure, National Water Development Agency have 
formulated National Perspective Plan for water resources development which 
envisages interlinking between various peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers 
for transfer of water from surplus basins to water deficit basins.

SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE: Sir, I beg to call the attention of 
the Minister of Disinvestment to the sale of BALCO at an abnormally 
low price and the questionable method of valuation of its assets. 
THE MINISTER OF STATE (INDEPENDENT CHARGE) OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): Sir. 
BALCO was referred for disinvestment- to the Disinvestment 
Commission by the United Front Government in 1996. Of the 58 units 
on which the Commission submitted recommendations, 38 were 
profit-making units. BALCO was one of these units. 
In the Report it submitted to the Government in April, 1997, 
the Disinvestment Commission re commended that the Government 
"immediately dismvest" -• these were the words -- its holding in the 
company "by offering a significant share of 40 per cent of the equity to 
a strategic partner, either domestic or foreign, through a transparent 
and competitive global bidding proces s". It further suggested that the 
Government within two years bring down its holding to 26 per cent 
and that, after that, it should keep the industry under, -- what it called -
- "an ongoing review" and 
215 

RAJYA SABHA    [27 February, 2001 ] 
disinvest its balance equity of 26 pe r cent at an appropriate time.    
This means that it would move out of the company completely. 
On June 12, 1998, the Chairman of the Disinvestment 
Commission, Mr. G.V. Ramakrishna wrote to the Government and 
recommended that the Go vernment consider se lling not 40 per cent, 
but 51 per cent of the equity to a st rategic partner, and also transfer 
management control to that partner. Sale of this magnitude and the 
transfer of management control, t he Chairman of the Disinvestment 
Commission wrote "will enable a smooth transaction with the 
participation of more bidders and better price for the shares." This is 
the recommendation which the Government accepted in March, 1999. 
The process of disinvestment in BALCO has thus been on for almost 
four years now. Detailed work on it has been going on 'for two years. 
The entire process has been conducted in public knowledge. The 
Disinvestment Policy has been discussed by the two Houses of 
Parliament in five lengthy debates in the last year and quarter. In the 
last two Sessions alone, more than 300 questions on disinvestment 
were answered. Since 30 ,h November, 1999, -- the only period that I 
could look up -- the fact that the Go vernment is disinvesting its equity 
holding in BALCO was specifically mentioned in written answers to 25 
questions. 
Open, competitive bidding has been the essential ingredient 
of the process at every stage, from the selection of the Advisor to that 
of the Strategic partner. The bid ders had been told that they must 
submit their bids by 4.00 p.m. on is" February. 2001. Two companies, 
namely. Hindalco and Sterlite, submitted bids in sealed covers to 
Secretary, Mines, befoio the deadl ine. These bids were kept 
confidential. The third party. ALCOA,  informed at that stage that it 
would not be submitting a bid. 
For a going concern, the appropriate method for valuation is 
the Discounted Cash Flow method. It assesses the future earning 
prospects of the company, discounts the stream of future earning to 
the present by a measur e of the opportunity cost of capital. This 
exercise naturally includes the cu rrent market share of the company, 
the valuation of its brand, the comp etition it is likely to face, the 
prospective price that it is liable to fetch for its products, the likely 
movement in its- costs, etc. For a bundant caution, the Advisers were 
asked to assess the value of the company by the two other universally 
recognised methods also. The Advisers undertook a detailed valuation 
exercise extending over several mont hs. For 51 per cent of equity, 
they placed the valuation through the Discounted Cash Flow method    
between    Rs.332    crores;    and    Rs.507    crores;    through    the 
216 

[27 February, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
Comparabie Valuation method bet ween Rs.299 crores and Rs.464 
crores and through the Balance Sheet method between Rs.305 crores 
and Rs.348 crores. 
Asset valuation is not an appropriate method for a going 
concern. It is used only when the concern is being shut, and its land, 
building, equipment, furniture, etc., are being disposed of. Even so, 
and in spite of the advice of Advisers, Government decided that the 
asset valuation of the company should also be done. For this purpose, 
the names of four firms were sent by the Advisers to BA1CO from 
among the list of Government approved valuers. A Screening 
Committee of BALCO selected P. V.  Rao & Co., through competitive 
bidding,( for valuing land and buildings and plant and machinery. The 
mines were valued by experts from  the Indian Bureau of Mines. The 
value of assets was placed around  Rs. 1,072 crores, 51 per cent of 
which would be around Rs.547 crores. The valuation by the three 
financial methods and the Asset Valuation were then submitted to the 
Evaluation Committee of the Government. After detailed deliberation, 
the Committee decided that the Discounted Cash Flow method was 
the appropriate one, that, for re asons they recorded, the Asset 
Valuation figure was somewhat on the high side. They decided that in 
addition a premium should be charged from the bidders as 
management too was being transferred. This is known as the Control 
Premium, Sir. Although the Advisor apprised them that the usual 
range for this premium is 10-15%. they decided to add 25%. By these 
steps they fixed the Reserve Price at Rs. 514.40 crore. 
In assessing these valuations and arriving at the Reserve 
Price, neither the valuers nor the Evaluation Committee knew the 
quantum of the bids. 
Once the Reserve Price . had been set, the bids were 
communicated to the Evaluation Committee. The bid of Hindalco was 
Rs. 275 crore. The bid of Sterlite was Rs. 551.5 crore. The Evaluation 
Committee recommended that the Ster lite bid be accepted, (i) It was 
twice the bid of Hindalco, and (n) it was above the Reserve Price 
which had been determined by the Committee. 
The report of the Evaluation Committee was sent to the inter -
Ministerial Group headed by Secretary (Mines), and then, after that, to 
the Core Group of Secretaries which is headed by the Cabinet 
Secretary. They considered the report and. endorsed the 
recommendation of the Evaluation Committee. 
217 

RAJYA SABHA    [27 February, 2001] 
The recommendation was then reported to the Cabinet 
Committee on Disinvestment which is presided over by the Prime 
Minister. The Committee accept ed the recommendations of the 
Evaluation Committee endorsed by the Inter-Ministerial Group and 
approved by the Core Group of Secr etaries, headed by the Cabinet 
Secretary. 
Meetings and consultations have been held with 
representatives of employees and special steps have been taken to 
protect their interests. Governm ent has ensured that clauses are 
included in the Shareholders' Agreement to safeguard the interests of 
workers. 
In accordance with the procedure which has already been 
announced in Parliament, once the transaction is completed, all 
documents and all papers relating to BALCO disinvestment, as in 
every other case, will be submitted to  the office of the Comptroller and 
Auditor General. In this case, as in every case of disinvestment, the 
CAG has agreed to kindly prepare a thorough assessment, and send it 
to Parliament and release it to the people.

In 1991, the Industrial Policy Resolution was moved, and,

my right side, articulated the policy of disinvestment of public sector 
enterprises. After that, a long period of ten years has passed. We,

position in regard to the ptoces s of disinvestment and aims and 
objectives of disinvestment. Keeping that in view, we wanted to have a

SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH (Andhra Pradesh):    Sir, thank 
you very much for giving me this opportunity to speak on this vital 
issue.   First of all, I want to ma ke it clear to the nation, as some 
AIADMK Members have pointed out, that we are not against 
disinvestment as such. Conceptually, we are for economic reforms. 
We are vigorously implementing the economic reforms in our State. I 
am happy to inform the House that our Chief Minister is a 
personification of economic reforms. If any Member has got any doubt 
about our attitude towards economic reforms, I want to make it clear to 
him. In fact, I have written two letters  to the Prime Minister, one in July 
and another in December, requesting him to appoint a Joint 
Parliamentary Committee or any other committee which would act like 
a watchdog, formulate the policy on disinvestment, and oversee and 
monitor the overall implementation of  the disinvestment policy. Now, 
there is a change in our economic scenario and economic philosophy. 
There was public sector and mixed economy. Now, we are throwing 
open our economy to market forces. At this juncture, what I am trying 
to say is that this is a transition period. We have been moving from a 
controlled economy to a market economy. In this scenario, unless we 
put in place effective safeguards, unless we act with utmost care and 
caution, there is every danger of the powerful, the influential, the 
corrupt and the mighty grabbing all the things to the detriment of the 
nation. It would create not only anarchy but also chaos in the 
economic sector. I hope nobody would welcome it, whether Right or 
Left, whether they belong to the Congress Party or the BJP. I think the 
hon. Members will concur with me. Sir, this request of mine to appoint 
a Joint Parliamentary Committee has been turned down by the Prime 
Minister. A letter was forwarded to the Minister for Disinvestment. He 
has replied to me. The Minister said, "We have laid down a 
transparent policy. 1 have answered umpteen questions on this 
subject on the floor of this House. In this scenario, I feel that there is 
no necessity for constituting such a Committee. However, after each 
transaction is completed, it will be referred to C&AG. As soon as the 
report is received from C&AG, it will be laid on the Table of the 
House." Whenever they want to incur any   expenditure or whenever 
they want to

SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, I thank you for giving me an opportunity to participate in 
this debate, I am opposed to the strategic sale that is going to be 
effected in respect of BALCO. Though the approach towards the 
public sector units had been discussed in Parliament several times, 
through several forms, I am sorry to say that so far, no consensus has 
been arrived at on disinvestment. es pecially disinvestment of the 
profit-making units. At the time of those discussions, Ministers said 
that the Government would protec t and modernise the profit-making 
public sector undertakings, but in the case of the units which are 
continuously incurring losses and f ound to be unviable, they would 
either be closed down or sold to the private sector . This assurance 
was given by the Ministers in the last  session. Of course, for the first 
time, in the last session, the Minister had said that all the entire public 
sector units would be sold within a ten year period. At no other time 
any Minister has said that. Even now Mr. Ramdas Agarwal was 
arguing that

the reason for disinvestment of the pu blic sector units is the fosses 
incurred by them. Regarding BALCO, it is a unit which could be 
considered to be in the core sector and which had been making profit 
year after year, till recently. And there is the possibility of this industry, 
this unit, working on a profit in futu re also. Moreover, this industry is 
having a reserve fund which comes to more than Rs.400 crores. And 
it has got huge assets. What is stat ed by the Minister is that the value 
of the assets will come up to an aggregate amount of Rs. 1072 crores. 
But no one can believe that. When you consider the entire land, the 
mines, the captive electricity generati ng plant and also the factories, 
no one can believe that it costs only that much. It has already been 
explained by several colleagues here as to the defects in the way the 
valuation has been effected. So I do not want to go into the details. In 
the case of such a company, what was the necessity for disinvesting 
and especially for making a strategic sale? It is not a unit which is 
running on loss continuously. Of course, modernisation may be 
required. Even if modernisation is required, it can generate funds from 
its own sources. Also, by depending on  other financial institutions it 
could have been done. It is not necessary to depend on anybody else 
for modernisation of the BALCO, if it is needed. Therefore, I cannot 
understand why this is being disinvested. especially, as a strategic 
sale. 
Then comes another question. One point that the hon. 
Minister has made for justifying th e strategic sale is that the 
Disinvestment Commission has recommended it. Of course, the 
Disinvestment Commission has recommended it. But the 
Disinvestment Commission's recommendations are not mandatory. 
The Government can approve or reject or partially approve or partially 
reject. In the same way, Parliament is also not bound to approve of it. 
Therefore, that is subject to the consideration of the Government and 
Parliament. Even though he is saying that the process was going on 
for the last four years, now during the last few months, it is found that 
there is a hurry in completing the pr ocess* In that process, a lot of 
suspicion has been generated. Generally, they say, regarding valuation, 
the recommendations of the Disinvestment Commission are accepted. 
The Disinvestment Commission itself  has stated how the valuation 
has to be done. In the case of calling for bidders, more bidders shall 
be there; the whole thing shall be done in a transparent way so that 
there shall not be any suspicion about the dealings. But all these 
conditions have not been observed by the Government in this 
particular transaction. Therefore, it  is highly objectionable. Moreover, 
this is an industry for which the lands acquired were tribal lands. The 
lands had been acquired and given over. They had

Another point is that the hon. Mi nister has made a general statement

protect their interests. As far as I know, the representatives of the 
union were called, and it can be said  that they have consulted them.
